analysis.title: Building the social contract for data center growth
key_insights: Hyperscale data center buildout has become a major issue in the 2026 US mid-term elections. The report cites an unverified survey in which a majority of respondents would rather live next to a nuclear power plant than a hyperscale data center.

The author lists several reasons for the hostility: fear of AI's impact, identification of the data center boom with President Trump, the scale of the buildings, and water use. The main reason cited is power demand at a time when energy prices pressure household budgets.

Premier Miton says 'user pays' (hyperscalers pay for the new generation they require) is the clear answer to the power problem, but argues hyperscalers must now do more to get a 'social license' to build.
The social license would require hyperscalers to fund generation and grid buildout beyond their own needs and to subsidize existing bill payers as a quid pro quo for operating in their communities.

Entergy's second-phase plan for Google's data center in West Memphis, Arkansas has Google paying the full cost of the new power resources it needs and funding grid investments. The plan produces $2.1 billion of net savings to other customers starting in 2028 over 20 years.

NiSource announced in October 2026 an expanded agreement around a Microsoft data center campus in Indiana. It would produce about $1.75 billion of savings for existing customers, which the company quantified as $140 per household per year.

American Electric Power has identified contracted load growth of 69 GW by 2030 across seven states, with 90% from data center customers. It forecasts up to $16 billion of cost offsets for existing residential customers as large-load customers contribute to fixed expenses.

Premier Miton sees the Entergy, NiSource and AEP frameworks as a roadmap for other utilities, and views utilities as the optimal way for infrastructure investors to benefit from the data center buildout.
The roadmap may not work in states where new generation is harder to build, political hostility is elevated or other regional factors apply.

sector_views.rationale: Utilities that build community consensus around data center load growth are seen as the optimal way for infrastructure investors to benefit from the hyperscale buildout.

risk_factors: Public and political hostility to hyperscale data centers, driven by electricity costs, AI fears, building scale and water use.
In some states and regions, new generation is harder to build or political hostility is higher, so the roadmap may not lead to the same result.
Household energy-price pressure could undermine community support for data center development.
geopolitical: Hyperscale data centers are an issue in the 2026 US mid-term elections, and the report links public hostility partly to the identification of the data center boom with President Trump.

tension_points.bull_case: Utilities such as Entergy, NiSource and AEP have built frameworks in which hyperscalers fund generation and grid buildout and deliver bill savings to existing customers, giving a roadmap to community support.
tension_points.bear_case: In states where new generation is harder to build or political hostility is elevated, the roadmap may not lead to the same result. Public hostility over power costs, AI, scale and water is strong.
